props.title: Frankenhooker
props.initialSlug: Mad scientist rebuilds girlfriend using hooker parts

sections.content: Frankenhooker (1990) stands as one of horror-comedy's most audacious B-movies, directed by exploitation master Frank Henenlotter (Basket Case (1982)). This twisted take on Mary Shelley's classic follows Jeffrey Franken, a mad scientist who decides to rebuild his dead fiancée using parts from New York City sex workers. The film's practical effects, particularly the explosive "super crack" scene where prostitutes literally explode, exemplifies the gonzo practical effects era of late 80s/early 90s horror. Like Henenlotter's other works, it combines sleazy Times Square aesthetics with genuine technical craftsmanship.

sections.content: The film sits within a specific subset of 1980s body horror that mixed dark comedy with practical effects spectacle. While Re-Animator (1985) took a more clinical approach to its mad science, and From Beyond (1986) leaned into cosmic horror, Frankenhooker embraces a sleazy urban exploitation vibe that feels directly connected to New York's grindhouse theater culture. The film's practical effects by Gabe Bartalos, who also worked on Basket Case 2 (1990) and Brain Damage (1988), represent a high point in low-budget practical effects innovation.

What sets Frankenhooker apart is its satirical edge regarding both the Frankenstein myth and the Times Square sex trade of the late 1980s. While films like Vice Squad (1982) and Fear City (1984) took serious approaches to similar subject matter, Henenlotter uses gallows humor and over-the-top gore to comment on exploitation itself. The film's influence can be seen in later horror-comedies like Return of the Living Dead III (1993) and Jack Frost (1997). SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Grindhouse Horror-Comedy

sections.content: Henenlotter's unique vision influenced a generation of filmmakers working in horror-comedy. Films like Dead Alive (1992) and Evil Ed (1995) followed similar formulas of excessive gore played for laughs. The practical effects renaissance in modern horror, seen in films like The Void (2016) and Psycho Goreman (2020), owes a debt to the DIY innovation of Frankenhooker and its contemporaries.
